Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Back and Thumb Pain
Description: Evaluation of localized low back pain and right thumb pain with review of preventive care.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient presents for annual followup and medication renewal, reporting approximately three months of persistent localized lumbar pain. It is typically rated 3 to 4 out of 10 but can become severe with twisting, bending, or changing position. There is no clear radicular pain down the legs. He has a remote history of lumbar problems and continues to perform physical work despite discomfort. He also reports one to two months of right thumb pain when gripping or squeezing. He is uncertain whether this represents arthritis or a strain. He recently lost part of a toenail. He is followed by Endocrinology for a parathyroid disorder and has scheduled laboratory monitoring.
PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Parathyroid disorder, chronic musculoskeletal complaints, hemorrhoids, and reflux symptoms controlled with medication.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Focal lumbar tenderness with pain reproduced by rotation and movement. Straight-leg maneuvers were not clearly suggestive of a radicular syndrome. Thumb grip strength was preserved; provocative carpal tunnel maneuvers were unrevealing, although localized thumb discomfort persisted. Partially detached toenail without signs of infection.
IMPRESSION AND PLAN:
1. Mechanical low back pain, possibly muscular or degenerative. Lumbar radiographs were ordered to assess for fracture or structural change. Acetaminophen was recommended as needed, and Flexeril was prescribed up to three times daily as needed for suspected spasm. The clinician expressed caution about ibuprofen in light of other medical considerations.
2. Right thumb pain, possibly degenerative joint disease. Right thumb or hand radiographs ordered. Conservative analgesia initially; reassess if persistent.
3. Detached toenail. No evidence of infection. Allow the remaining loose nail to separate naturally; regrowth may take time.
4. Preventive care. Zoster vaccination was recommended and to be scheduled separately. Routine endocrine laboratory testing remains due at the previously designated time.
The patient will be contacted for unexpected x-ray findings and return in six months or sooner for persistent symptoms.
